faults.name: Connection pool exhaustion
faults.summary: Callers hold connections longer than the pool can recycle them. Wait time climbs first, available connections reach zero, and every upstream caller then times out together.

faults.name: Cache stampede after mass eviction
faults.summary: A mass eviction empties the working set, every request misses at once, and the traffic that the cache was absorbing lands on the origin in a single wave.

faults.name: Consumer group lag growth
faults.summary: Consumers fall behind producers. Nothing errors, so alerting on error rate sees a healthy system while downstream data quietly goes stale.

faults.name: Heap growth with escalating pause time
faults.summary: Resident memory climbs monotonically across a deploy window. Collection pauses lengthen as the heap fills, and the process is eventually restarted by the platform, which resets the graph and hides the trend.

faults.name: Synchronous timeout cascade
faults.summary: One slow synchronous dependency occupies caller threads until the caller itself runs out. Retries multiply the load on the already-slow dependency, so the system degrades faster the harder it tries to recover.

faults.name: TLS certificate expiry
faults.summary: A certificate reaches its expiry. Failure is total and instant at the moment of expiry rather than gradual, which is what distinguishes it from a capacity problem on the same graph.

faults.name: Query amplification after deploy
faults.summary: Request volume is unchanged but query volume is not. A change replaced a batched read with a per-item read, so cost scales with result size rather than with traffic.

faults.name: Search shard imbalance
faults.summary: Documents concentrate on one shard. Mean latency stays acceptable and the tail does not, so a dashboard built on averages shows nothing wrong.

mechanisms.example: what is the connection pool ceiling for events-bus
mechanisms.label: unanswerable
mechanisms.note: The sharpest trick in the set. Takes a property the corpus documents for ONE service and asks it of a different service. Retrieval happily returns the passage about the wrong service, so a weak system answers confidently with a real number that is about something else.

mechanisms.example: cache.evictions_per_s is climbing on sessions-cache, what is happening
mechanisms.label: answerable
mechanisms.note: Takes a real metric from a fault pattern and asks about it the way an on-call engineer would. Answerable because the runbook for that fault is in the corpus.

mechanisms.label: answerable
mechanisms.note: Turns a heading in a document into the question that heading answers. Answerable by construction — the section IS the answer.

mechanisms.example: what was the impact of pricing rounding change applied to all regions at once
mechanisms.label: answerable
mechanisms.note: The same idea narrowed to runbooks, where headings are procedural steps.

mechanisms.example: what is the expected process.memory.rss_mb baseline on edge-gateway
mechanisms.label: unanswerable
mechanisms.note: Asks about a fault a given service physically cannot have — a memory-leak metric on a gateway that does not run that way. Plausible-sounding, ungrounded.

mechanisms.example: what severity is a tier 0 service being unavailable
mechanisms.label: answerable
mechanisms.note: Asks for a specific number a policy states — a severity level, an escalation timer. The hardest answerable kind, because a near-miss reads as correct.

mechanisms.example: the disk is full on the host, what should I do
mechanisms.label: unanswerable
mechanisms.note: Topics deliberately left out of the corpus entirely, listed in GAPS.md. Absence is VERIFIED against the text, not assumed.
